evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.
4. **What must remain my decision or another person’s responsibility?** Name the value judgment, permission or professional check that cannot be delegated.

OpenAI calls listening and speaking at the same time full duplex. GPT-Live-1 can keep listening when a caller pauses, interrupts or changes direction. aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Why can a GPT-Live-1 call sound perfectly handled and yet leave you with no reservation?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: Because the voice layer only manages the conversation — listening and speaking at once, absorbing interruptions — while a separate backend application checks availability, applies the business's rules and writes the booking record. If the backend never receives, validates or stores the request, the smooth conversation produced nothing durable; the application, not the voice, owns confirmations and the lasting record.
aiEditorialAnalysis.expectedEvidence: P004 states the application owns permissions, confirmations and the lasting record; P005 shows the booking tool and availability data determining whether a table is recorded.
aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; a nontechnical reader could reproduce it after one reading.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Using the article's mechanism, what most likely went wrong and what should the caller have done on the call?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: The voice layer smoothly absorbed the mid-sentence dosage change, but the backend pharmacy system — which owns the durable refill record and must apply prescription rules — either never received the amended request as a tool action or rejected it under a rule the voice glossed over. Fluency masked a missing record. The caller should have asked the system to read back both medications, dosages and pickup times and to provide the confirmation numbers, and asked for a pharmacist if it could not.

aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The article's voice-versus-record model resolves this unseen case without any additional concepts, confirming genuine transferability.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI released GPT-Live-1 to developers through its API on September 10. The same day, Yelp said it had integrated the voice model into Yelp Host, which answers restaurant calls, and Hatch, which handles calls for service businesses such as repair companies.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: The OpenAI release excerpt states a September 10, 2026 launch of GPT-Live-1 in the API for developers, matching P002 exactly.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: September 10, 2026: OpenAI says it is launching GPT-Live-1 in the API for developers building voice-enabled apps and business workflows.
OpenAI describes GPT-Live-1 as capable of listening and speaking at the same time, with deeper reasoning and actions delegated to models and tools paired with it.

Traditional voice agents stitch together speech-to-text, a reasoning model, and text-to-speech. Each handoff adds latency and creates more opportunities to lose timing, context, or the natural rhythm of a conversation.
OpenAI lists telephony support for phone calls from restaurant reservations to customer support.
OpenAI says GPT-Live-1 is available in the API at $0.05 per minute for the front-end voice layer; the backend model and agent harness remain separate parts of the product.
OpenAI presents smoother interruption handling, background-noise handling and longer-session reliability as product strengths and reports its own evaluations and customer statements.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Yelp announced that it integrated GPT-Live-1 into Yelp Host, its voice AI solution for restaurants, and Hatch, its communications platform for service businesses.
Yelp describes GPT-Live-1 as the front-end voice layer that interacts directly with callers while Yelp Host and Hatch supply business data and operational intelligence.
The company says callers can interrupt, change topics mid-sentence or speak to people in the background while the voice system adapts.
Yelp says initial production testing showed improved call handling and fewer call transfers, but the release provides no sample size, method, geographic rollout or independent evaluation.
Yelp says this is reflected in more Yelp Host callers speaking in full, natural sentences during early testing, rather than short voice commands.

The release says Yelp Host has handled more than one million calls since launching in October 2025. That is product history spanning the period before this September 2026 integration announcement, not a GPT-Live-1 performance count.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: This is where someone who never opens an API may encounter the release: while making a reservation, changing a food order or arranging an appointment by phone. OpenAI calls listening and speaking at the same time full duplex. GPT-Live-1 can keep listening when a caller pauses, interrupts or changes direction. A separate backend system still checks business information, applies rules and uses tools. OpenAI’s documentation says the application—not the voice model—owns permissions, confirmations and the lasting record of a task.
